subtopic_detail: low voltage electrocardiogram with increased wall thickness and nephrotic range proteinuria in an infiltrative cardiomyopathy
stem:
You are the cardiology registrar assessing a 64 year old man referred with five months of breathlessness on exertion and ankle swelling. He has lost 8 kg without trying and feels light headed whenever he stands up quickly.

His wife mentions that he has twice woken with purple marks around his eyes after a bout of coughing, and that his tongue looks bigger than it used to. He has never had hypertension and his blood pressure has in fact been running lower than his usual over the past year, so his general practitioner stopped his only antihypertensive six months ago. There is no family history of cardiac disease or sudden death. His investigations are back.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, blood pressure 98/64 lying with a 28 mmHg systolic fall on standing, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 96 per cent in air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Elevated jugular venous pressure, bilateral pitting oedema to the knees, macroglossia with lateral dental indentations, periorbital purpura
data_table.Investigations: Urine protein to creatinine ratio 420 mg/mmol (less than 30), serum albumin 24 g/L (35 to 50), estimated glomerular filtration rate 55 mL/min/1.73m2 (greater than 60), N terminal pro B type natriuretic peptide markedly raised, high sensitivity troponin persistently mildly raised without a rise and fall pattern
data_table.Electrocardiogram: Sinus rhythm with low voltage QRS complexes in the limb leads and poor R wave progression
data_table.Echocardiogram: Left ventricular wall thickness 16 mm, ejection fraction 52 per cent, grade 2 diastolic dysfunction, biatrial enlargement, apical sparing on longitudinal strain imaging

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Technetium labelled bone scintigraphy to characterise the cardiac deposits
options.rationale: Bone avid tracer uptake identifies the transthyretin form of the disease and is an excellent non invasive test for it, which makes this the strongest competing answer. It must not be used alone, because a positive scan is only interpretable as transthyretin disease once a plasma cell disorder has been excluded, and the extracardiac features here point to the light chain form. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging with late gadolinium enhancement now
options.rationale: Diffuse subendocardial late enhancement with abnormal gadolinium kinetics supports infiltration and refines the cardiac assessment, so this is a reasonable investigation at some point. It cannot distinguish the light chain from the transthyretin form, and that distinction is the one that changes treatment. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Serum free light chain assay with serum and urine immunofixation studies
options.rationale: Macroglossia, periorbital purpura and nephrotic range proteinuria alongside an infiltrative cardiomyopathy indicate light chain deposition from an underlying plasma cell disorder, and the light chain assay with immunofixation is both the most sensitive screen and the test that determines treatment. Identifying the clonal process is what separates a haematologically treatable disease from an untreatable one, and it must precede or accompany any bone scintigraphy. (Source: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Percutaneous renal biopsy to establish the cause of the proteinuria
options.rationale: A renal biopsy would demonstrate the deposits and is sometimes how the diagnosis is first made, but it is invasive and carries bleeding risk that is increased in this disease by factor X deficiency and vascular fragility. A blood and urine based assay answers the same question first. (Source: Kidney Health Australia)

options.text: Invasive coronary angiography to exclude an ischaemic cardiomyopathy
options.rationale: The persistently raised troponin without a rise and fall pattern reflects ongoing myocardial injury from infiltration rather than plaque rupture, and the preserved ejection fraction with marked wall thickening and biatrial enlargement is not an ischaemic pattern. Angiography also exposes him to contrast with an already reduced filtration rate. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

explanation.summary: Infiltrative cardiomyopathy should be suspected whenever increased left ventricular wall thickness coexists with low QRS voltages, because hypertensive and hypertrophic disease both produce high voltages in proportion to muscle mass and the discordance signals that the thickening is deposited material rather than myocyte hypertrophy. Apical sparing on longitudinal strain imaging, biatrial enlargement, a persistently raised troponin without a rise and fall pattern and disproportionately elevated natriuretic peptides complete the echocardiographic and biochemical picture. The critical fork is between the light chain form arising from a clonal plasma cell population and the transthyretin form, because the first is treated with anti plasma cell therapy and carries a far worse untreated prognosis measured in months, while the second is treated with a transthyretin stabiliser. Extracardiac features separate them: macroglossia, periorbital purpura and nephrotic range proteinuria are essentially specific to the light chain form, while bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome and lumbar spinal stenosis years earlier suggest transthyretin disease. A further trap is that blood pressure often falls and antihypertensives are withdrawn in the year before diagnosis, and autonomic involvement produces the postural drop seen here.
key_points: Increased wall thickness with low QRS voltage is the signature discordance of infiltration
Apical sparing on strain imaging and biatrial enlargement support the diagnosis
Macroglossia, periorbital purpura and nephrotic proteinuria indicate the light chain form
Exclude a plasma cell disorder before interpreting bone scintigraphy as transthyretin disease
A persistently raised troponin without a rise and fall pattern reflects infiltration, not plaque rupture
explanation.pearls: Serum free light chains with serum and urine immunofixation together detect over ninety per cent of light chain amyloidosis, whereas serum protein electrophoresis alone misses roughly a third, so ordering electrophoresis by itself is the commonest way this diagnosis is delayed.

sources.label: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand
Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand

subtopic_detail: treating on the basis of a minimal trauma fracture when the bone density score is in the osteopenic range
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 62 year old woman six weeks after she tripped on a flat footpath outside the shops and broke her wrist. She fell from standing height onto her outstretched hand and the fracture has been managed in a cast, which has now come off.

Her last menstrual period was at 51. She has never smoked, drinks two standard drinks a week and walks most days. She has never taken oral corticosteroids. Her mother broke her hip at 74. Her body mass index is 22 kg/m2. You arranged a bone density scan and screening bloods after the fracture and the results are now available.

data_table.Examination: No thoracic kyphosis, height unchanged from her recorded height five years ago, wrist fracture united with good range of movement
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium within normal limits, 25 hydroxyvitamin D within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, renal function within normal limits, serum protein electrophoresis shows no paraprotein
data_table.Bone densitometry: Femoral neck T score minus 2.3, lumbar spine T score minus 2.1

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Lifestyle advice with a repeat bone density scan in two years
options.rationale: This is the correct approach for a woman with this T score and no fracture, which is exactly why it is tempting. A fracture from a fall at standing height after the age of 50 establishes the diagnosis independently of the densitometry and identifies her as being at high risk of a further fracture in the next two years. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners Osteoporosis Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners Osteoporosis Guideline

options.text: Commence six monthly denosumab injections as initial therapy
options.rationale: Denosumab is an effective antiresorptive and is used where bisphosphonates are contraindicated, not tolerated or ineffective. It requires strict continuity, because stopping it without transitioning to another agent produces rapid bone loss and a risk of multiple vertebral fractures, so it is not the first choice in an otherwise straightforward case. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Commence menopausal hormone therapy for bone protection alone
options.rationale: Hormone therapy does preserve bone density and reduces fracture, and it is a reasonable choice for a woman in her early fifties who also has vasomotor symptoms. At 62 and eleven years past her final period it is not started for bone protection alone, because the balance of cardiovascular and thrombotic risk shifts with time since menopause. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society)

options.text: Commence an oral bisphosphonate with calcium and vitamin D advice
options.rationale: A minimal trauma fracture after 50 defines osteoporosis clinically whatever the T score shows, and it is also the criterion under which antiresorptive therapy is subsidised in Australia. Oral bisphosphonate is the first line agent, with adequate calcium intake and vitamin D as supportive measures rather than as treatment in themselves. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners Osteoporosis Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners Osteoporosis Guideline

options.text: Commence calcium and vitamin D supplements without other therapy
options.rationale: Calcium and vitamin D support the action of antiresorptive therapy but do not meaningfully reduce fracture risk on their own in someone who has already sustained a minimal trauma fracture. Her vitamin D is already within normal limits. (Source: Healthy Bones Australia)

explanation.summary: A minimal trauma fracture is one sustained from a fall at standing height or less, and after the age of 50 it establishes a clinical diagnosis of osteoporosis regardless of the bone density result, which matters because around half of all fragility fractures occur in people whose T score falls in the osteopenic range rather than below minus 2.5. The single strongest predictor of a future fracture is a past fracture, and the risk is highest in the first two years afterwards, a window often described as the imminent fracture risk period. This is the rationale for fracture liaison services and for starting treatment promptly rather than waiting for a densitometry threshold to be crossed. Secondary causes should be screened for before treatment, covering calcium, vitamin D, renal and thyroid function, and a paraprotein, with coeliac serology and testosterone considered in selected patients. Oral bisphosphonates are first line in Australia, with adherence being the main practical limitation, and denosumab or an anabolic agent reserved for intolerance, contraindication or very high risk.
key_points: A fall from standing height causing fracture after 50 defines osteoporosis clinically
Around half of fragility fractures occur in people with osteopenic rather than osteoporotic scores
Risk of a further fracture is highest in the first two years
Screen for secondary causes before starting treatment
Denosumab requires strict continuity because cessation causes rapid bone loss
explanation.pearls: Never stop denosumab without transitioning to a bisphosphonate, because the rebound increase in bone turnover after a missed six monthly dose can cause multiple vertebral fractures within a year, a risk that does not follow cessation of bisphosphonate therapy.

sources.label: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners Osteoporosis Guideline

subtopic_detail: first line medical treatment for heavy painful bleeding with diffuse myometrial changes on ultrasound
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar in the outpatient clinic seeing a 42 year old woman with three years of periods that have become progressively heavier and more painful. She now floods through a pad hourly on her worst two days and the cramping starts two days before any bleeding appears.

She has had two vaginal births and has not been pregnant for nine years. She has taken over the counter ibuprofen with limited benefit. On bimanual examination the uterus is bulky and globular, about the size of a ten week pregnancy, tender to palpation and mobile, with no separate adnexal mass. Her transvaginal ultrasound and bloods are available.

data_table.Examination: Uterus bulky and globular at approximately ten week size, tender on bimanual palpation, mobile with no adnexal mass, cervix appears normal
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 104 g/L (115 to 165), ferritin 9 micrograms/L (15 to 200), thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, cervical screening test up to date and negative
data_table.Imaging: Transvaginal ultrasound shows a globally enlarged uterus with asymmetrical myometrial thickening, small myometrial cysts and an indistinct junctional zone; no discrete fibroid identified; endometrial thickness 6 mm; ovaries normal

lead_in: What would you first recommend as treatment?

options.text: A gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist with add back therapy
options.rationale: Induced hypo-oestrogenism does shrink the uterus and reduce bleeding, but it is used for short term control before surgery rather than as ongoing treatment because of bone loss and vasomotor effects. Symptoms return once it is stopped. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Referral for total hysterectomy at the next available list
options.rationale: Hysterectomy is definitive and is appropriate where medical treatment fails or is declined, but proceeding to major surgery before any hormonal treatment has been tried is a substantial escalation. Most women in this situation obtain adequate control medically. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: A continuous combined oral contraceptive pill regimen
options.rationale: Continuous combined oral contraception is a reasonable second line option that reduces bleeding and dysmenorrhoea, and it suits women who prefer an oral method. It is less effective than the intrauterine route for heavy bleeding and carries a thrombotic risk that the local method does not. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Tranexamic acid taken during the days of heavy bleeding
options.rationale: Antifibrinolytic therapy reduces bleeding volume by around a third and is useful as an adjunct or for women wanting non hormonal treatment. It does nothing for the dysmenorrhoea, which is half of her problem here. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Insertion of a levonorgestrel releasing intrauterine system
options.rationale: Local progestogen delivery thins the endometrium and acts directly on the myometrium, reducing both bleeding volume and the associated pain, and it is the recommended first line treatment for this condition. It also treats the iron deficiency driver by reducing ongoing loss. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

explanation.summary: Adenomyosis is the presence of endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium with surrounding smooth muscle hypertrophy, and it classically presents in the fourth and fifth decades with the combination of heavy menstrual bleeding and progressive secondary dysmenorrhoea that begins before the bleeding starts. Examination typically finds a diffusely bulky, globular and tender uterus, in contrast to the irregular firm non tender uterus of fibroid disease, and this distinction carries through to imaging. The ultrasound features are asymmetrical myometrial thickening, myometrial cysts, subendometrial echogenic lines and buds, and an indistinct or thickened junctional zone, with magnetic resonance imaging reserved for cases where ultrasound is equivocal or surgical planning is needed. Because the process is diffuse rather than focal, treatments directed at discrete lesions such as myomectomy or uterine artery embolisation are less reliable than they are for fibroids. The levonorgestrel releasing intrauterine system is first line, combined hormonal or continuous progestogen therapy is second line, and hysterectomy remains definitive for women who have completed their family and in whom medical management has failed.
key_points: Heavy bleeding with dysmenorrhoea starting before the bleeding is the characteristic pattern
A globular tender bulky uterus contrasts with the irregular firm uterus of fibroids
Ultrasound shows myometrial cysts and an indistinct junctional zone without a discrete lesion
The levonorgestrel releasing intrauterine system is first line treatment
Check ferritin, because iron deficiency is usually present before anaemia appears
explanation.pearls: Check ferritin as well as haemoglobin in every woman with heavy menstrual bleeding, because iron stores are exhausted long before the haemoglobin falls and treating the deficiency resolves the fatigue that patients often attribute to the bleeding itself.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists
